218.title: An-Nazi'at: fear of standing
218.hook: whoever feared standing before his Lord and held the self from desire, the garden is home (79:40–41)
218.howItsDone: Muslims describe this as struggle with the self (jihad an-nafs): fasting, lowering the gaze, and holding the tongue in anger are all practiced as small, daily ways of restraining the self from whim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in An-Nazi'at: Musa sent to Pharaoh, told to open with a question. Your line was would you purify yourself. Did you offer someone a gentle question instead of a verdict? Day two hundred eighteen.

It's eleven at night. The phone is in your hand, and the thumb already knows the way. One more video. One more scroll. A second slice. The reply you'd regret by morning, typed and waiting for the send button. Everyone knows this moment, the tiny gap between wanting something and doing it. Most days the gap is so small we don't notice it's there. Surah An-Nazi'at, which we've been reading for three days, ends its argument inside exactly that gap. After the great upheaval and the story of Musa and Pharaoh, it sorts people into two, and the second group is described by what they did in that small moment. Today: the fear of standing, and holding the self back.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, PHONE IN HAND.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN WANTING AND DOING.` → `WHERE THE SURAH ENDS ITS ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: First the other group. The surah says whoever rebelled and chose the life of this world, the fire is home. Then the turn. Here is Pickthall's translation: But as for him who feared to stand before his Lord and restrained his soul from lust, Lo! the Garden will be his home. Two things, then. The first is a fear, and it's a specific one: maqam rabbihi, the standing before his Lord. Commentators read the phrase two ways. Some say it means the Day when every person will stand before Allah to give an account. Others say it means Allah standing over a person now, seeing what they do in the dark. Either way, it's the awareness of being seen, and it works like a light switched on in a room. The second thing is the holding. The soul, the nafs, held back from al-hawa. Pickthall says lust, but hawa is wider than that. It's the pull of whim, the wind that blows the self wherever it likes. The Arabic word for air, hawa', is built from the same letters. Notice what's not being said. Desire isn't evil. Food, sleep, love and rest are all gifts in the Qur'an. The problem is the self steered only by the wind. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ put it in a picture Bukhari records: the strong one isn't the wrestler who throws people down; the strong one controls himself when angry. And one small word at the end: home. Not reward, not prize. The Garden is where this person lives. That closes the long surahs at the front of the juz' for us.
screen: `TWO GROUPS, TWO HOMES.` · `MAQAM — THE STANDING BEFORE HIS LORD.` · `HAWA — THE SELF BLOWN BY WHIM.` · `THE STRONG ONE HOLDS BACK.` · then, large: `HOLD THE SELF BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and pick one small desire you already know will come today. The snack at four. The extra hour of scrolling. The sharp reply. Picture the moment it arrives. Now picture the gap, the half second before you act, and stay in it. Breathe slowly into that gap and let it get a little wider. Nothing is being taken from you. You're only noticing that you can choose. If you pray, you can bring to mind the standing before your Lord while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
An-Nazi'at. Those who pull out, the surah that ends by sorting people by what they did with the gap: the ones who held the self back from whim. Today's word.
Your line: hold the self back. Once today, refuse one small desire, not forever, just this once, and notice who was doing the choosing. Day two hundred eighteen.

219.title: An-Naba': the great news
219.hook: what are they asking about, the great news (78:1–2)
219.howItsDone: Surah an-Naba' opens the thirtieth part of the Qur'an, and many Muslims memorize it as children; it is often recited in the prayers, and the whole juz' is named after its first word, 'amma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of An-Nazi'at: the one who feared the standing before his Lord. Your line was hold the self back. Did you catch the gap before one small desire, and choose? Day two hundred nineteen.

Picture a town where everyone is talking about the same thing. At the market, at the well, in the evenings. Some laugh about it. Some are angry. Some are quietly unsettled and won't admit it. That was Mecca when this surah came. A man in their own town was saying that after death every person would be raised and would stand to give an account. People argued about it the way a whole city argues about one piece of news. And the surah opens by stepping into the noise and asking a question of its own. It's the first surah of the juz' we've been reading backward, and its first word gives the whole juz' its name. Today: An-Naba', the great news.
screen: `A WHOLE TOWN ARGUING.` → `ONE PIECE OF NEWS.` → `THE FIRST SURAH OF THE JUZ'.`

segments.voice: The surah begins: 'amma yatasa'alun. About what are they asking one another? 'Amma is two little words run together, 'an ma, about what. It's the word that names the whole thirtieth part of the Qur'an: Juz' 'Amma, the part that begins with about what. Then the surah answers its own question: about the great news, an-naba' al-'azim, the one they disagree about. Pickthall calls it the awful tidings, awful in the old sense, full of awe. Arabic has an everyday word for news, khabar. Naba' is heavier. Classical scholars of the language describe naba' as news of great weight, news that brings real knowledge and changes something. You don't use naba' for the weather. What is the great news? Most commentators say it's the Resurrection, the raising of the dead and the Day of account, which the people of Mecca found hardest to accept. Some early commentators said it was the Qur'an itself, or the preaching of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. All three hang together: a book, brought by a messenger, announcing a Day. Then comes a line said twice, and the repetition is the point: no, they will come to know; then no, they will come to know. The surah doesn't mock the question. It takes it as the biggest question a person can ask, and then, instead of arguing, it turns toward the world and starts pointing. We'll follow that pointing tomorrow. For today, notice this: the Qur'an's last part opens not with a command, but with a question people were already asking.
screen: `'AMMA — ABOUT WHAT?` · `NABA' — NEWS OF GREAT WEIGHT.` · `THE RESURRECTION, THE BOOK, THE MESSENGER.` · `THEY WILL COME TO KNOW.` · then, large: `THE GREAT NEWS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the noise of the day settle a little. Then ask yourself the surah's question: about what am I asking? Underneath the small questions, what to eat, what to say, what to reply, there is usually one big one. Maybe it's about death, or meaning, or whether you're loved, or what comes after. Don't answer it. Just find it and name it quietly, in a few words. Let it sit with you, the way the surah lets its question sit. The bell holds the time.
An-Naba'. The news, news of great weight: the name of Surah 78, the first surah of the thirtieth part, which opens with the question about what. Today's word.
Your line: the great news. Today, when you hear someone arguing about the news, remember the one the surah means, and ask yourself what your own big question is. Day two hundred nineteen.

220.title: An-Naba': sleep as rest
220.hook: We made the earth a bed, mountains as pegs, sleep for rest, the night a cover (78:6–10)
220.howItsDone: Many Muslims follow the Prophet's bedtime practice: making wudu, lying on the right side, and saying bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya (in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live), with a phrase of praise for being given life again on waking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of An-Naba': about what are they asking? Your line was the great news. Did you find the one big question underneath the small ones? Day two hundred twenty.

Think about last night. At some point you lay down, the thoughts slowed, and then, without deciding to, you were gone. Hours passed that you can't account for. Then you were back, the same person, in the same bed, as if someone had pressed pause and then play. We do this every single night of our lives and almost never think about it. Yesterday the surah asked what people were arguing about, the great news of a Day when the dead are raised. Today it answers, and the answer surprises people. It doesn't argue at all. It points. At the ground under you, the mountains, and your own pillow. Today: sleep as rest.
screen: `PAUSE, THEN PLAY.` → `EVERY NIGHT OF YOUR LIFE.` → `THE SURAH STOPS ARGUING AND POINTS.`

segments.voice: The surah asks a run of questions, and each one is a picture. Have We not made the earth a resting place, mihad, a word also used for a cradle or a spread bed? And the mountains as pegs, awtad, like the pegs that hold a tent down in the wind. And created you in pairs. Then the line we're here for: wa ja'alna nawmakum subata. And We made your sleep subat. Subat comes from a root that means to cut off, to stop, to rest. It's related to the word for the Sabbath, the day of rest. Sleep is the cutting off: the day's work and worry stop, and the body is repaired. Then the night as a garment, libas, the same word for clothing, wrapping you like a cover. And the day for earning a living. The argument is quiet but clear. You worry that raising the dead is impossible? You go through a small version every night. Another verse, in Surah az-Zumar, says Allah takes the souls at the time of death, and takes those that have not died during their sleep, then keeps some and sends the others back until an appointed time. Many Muslims mark this at the edges of each night. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Bukhari records, would say at bedtime, in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. And on waking, praise to Allah who gave us life after He had made us die, and to Him is the rising. Every morning, a rehearsal of the great news.
screen: `THE EARTH A BED, MOUNTAINS AS PEGS.` · `SUBAT — SLEEP AS THE CUTTING OFF.` · `THE NIGHT AS A GARMENT.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL RAISING.` · then, large: `SLEEP IS A SIGN.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whichever your body wants. Let your eyes close. Start at your feet and let them go heavy, as if the earth really were a bed underneath them. Then your legs, your back, your shoulders, your jaw. Feel the parts of you that have been working all day, and let each one stop. That's subat, the cutting off, in miniature. If you pray, you can say quietly, in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. Then just rest. The bell holds the time.
An-Naba'. The great news, and the surah that answers it by pointing at the world: the earth a bed, the night a garment, and sleep made for rest. Today's word.
Your line: sleep is a sign. Tonight, go to bed a little earlier than usual, and when you wake tomorrow, notice for one second that you came back. Day two hundred twenty.

221.title: An-Naba': the Day of sorting
221.hook: the Day the trumpet sounds and you come in crowds (78:17–18)
221.howItsDone: Belief in the Last Day is one of the pillars of faith in Islam; Muslims recite surahs like an-Naba' in prayer and speak of the Day with both hope and fear, often reflecting on their deeds before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the middle of An-Naba': the earth a bed, the night a garment. Your line was sleep is a sign. Did you go to bed early, and notice that you came back this morning? Day two hundred twenty-one.

Think of a drawer you've been stuffing for years. Receipts, cables, a birthday card, a key to nothing. Everything's in there together, and you can't tell the treasure from the junk anymore. Then one Saturday you pour it all out onto the table and sort it. What matters goes in one pile. What doesn't goes in another. Things you'd forgotten turn up. A life can feel like that drawer: kindnesses and cruelties, the good day and the bad one, all mixed. An-Naba' has asked its question and pointed at the signs. Now it names the Day itself, and the name it chooses is a sorting word. Today: the Day of sorting.
screen: `A DRAWER STUFFED FOR YEARS.` → `POURED OUT AND SORTED.` → `THE SURAH NAMES THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The verse says: inna yawm al-fasli kana miqata. The Day of fasl is an appointed time. Fasl comes from a root meaning to separate, to divide, to tell one thing from another. Pickthall translates it as Decision; others say Sorting or Judgment. In everyday Arabic the same root gives the word for a chapter of a book and for a season of the year: a section cut off from the rest. So the Day of fasl is the day when what was mixed is separated, and each thing is seen for what it was. Then the picture: the day the trumpet is blown and you come in crowds, afwaja, wave after wave of people. Later the surah shows the Spirit and the angels standing in ranks, and no one speaks except whom the Most Merciful permits, and they say what is right. And it ends with one of the Qur'an's most human lines. On that Day a person will look at what their own hands sent ahead. What their hands sent ahead: every act has already gone on before them, waiting. And the one who denied it all will say, if only I were dust. The surah describes the garden too, for the ones who were mindful, with gardens and cups and no idle talk. Muslims hold the Day with both hope and fear. The point of naming it isn't to scare anyone into a corner. It's that nothing you did is lost in the drawer. Every small kindness gets found.
screen: `FASL — TO SEPARATE, TO SORT.` · `A CHAPTER, A SEASON, A DAY.` · `CROWDS, AND ANGELS IN RANKS.` · `WHAT YOUR HANDS SENT AHEAD.` · then, large: `THE DAY OF SORTING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe slowly. Now think of your days as a long line behind you, all the way back. Don't judge them. Just let a few rise up: one you're proud of, one you'd rather forget, one ordinary afternoon you'd almost lost. Notice that all of them are yours, and all of them went on ahead. Then think of today, which is still being written. What would you like your hands to send ahead from this one? One small thing is enough. The bell holds the time.
An-Naba'. The great news, and the surah that ends by naming the Day of sorting, when each person sees what their hands sent ahead. Today's word.
Your line: the day of sorting. Once today, before you do something, ask which pile it belongs in, and choose one thing worth sending ahead. Day two hundred twenty-one.

222.title: Juz' 'Amma, the shape
222.hook: thirty-seven surahs: the Day, the orphan, the soul, the One
222.howItsDone: Most Muslim children learn Juz' 'Amma first, often from its end (An-Nas) backward, and its short surahs are the ones most often recited in the daily prayers; the thirty-part division lets many read the whole Qur'an across a month, especially in Ramadan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of An-Naba': the Day of fasl, when what was mixed is separated. Your line was the day of sorting. What did you choose to send ahead? Day two hundred twenty-two.

When you finish a hike, there's a moment near the top when you turn around. The path you climbed is all laid out below you, and for the first time you can see its shape: where it switched back, where it got steep, where you stopped for water. Since day one hundred fifty-nine we've been walking backward through the last part of the Qur'an, from An-Nas on its final page to An-Naba' at the front. Yesterday we reached the start. So today we don't read a new surah. We turn around and look at the whole thing. Thirty-seven surahs, and four things they keep coming back to. Today: Juz' 'Amma, the shape.
screen: `TURNING AROUND NEAR THE TOP.` → `FROM AN-NAS BACK TO AN-NABA'.` → `THE WHOLE PATH IN VIEW.`

segments.voice: First, what a juz' is. Juz' means a part. The Qur'an has one hundred fourteen surahs of very different lengths, and at some point after the Prophet's time, Muslims divided it into thirty parts of roughly equal length, so it could be read in a month, a part a day. That's why so many people finish the whole Qur'an in Ramadan. The division is a reading aid, not part of the revelation itself. The thirtieth part runs from Surah seventy-eight to the end, thirty-seven surahs, and it's named for its first word, 'amma, about what. Most of these surahs are counted as Meccan, from the early years. They're short, they rhyme, and many open with oaths: by the dawn, by the sun, by the fig and the olive. And under all that sound, four themes keep returning. The Day: An-Naba', Az-Zalzalah, Al-Qari'ah, the sorting and the weighing. The orphan: again and again the surahs ask who fed the orphan and who pushed him away, from Ad-Duha to Al-Ma'un. The soul: Ash-Shams swears by the soul and the One who shaped it, and says whoever purifies it has succeeded. And the One: Al-Ikhlas, four short lines on the oneness of Allah. The Day, the orphan, the soul, the One. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came from an orphan's childhood himself, which gives the orphan verses a sound all their own. This is the part children usually memorize first, and the part most often heard in the daily prayers. Short enough to learn. Deep enough to keep for life.

segments.voice: Sit, and let the last few weeks come back to you, one surah at a time. The whisperer that withdraws. Daybreak. Say, He is Allah, the One. The morning light of Ad-Duha. The man who frowned. The trumpet and the crowds. Don't try to remember them all. Just notice which ones come back on their own, the ones that stuck. Pick three. Hold their names in your mind, and ask yourself what each one gave you. The bell holds the time.
Juz' 'Amma. The thirtieth part of the Qur'an, thirty-seven surahs named for their first word: the Day, the orphan, the soul, the One. Today's word.
Your line: the whole juz'. Today, write down your three favorite surahs from this part, and one line about why each one stayed with you. Day two hundred twenty-two.

223.title: Reciting in prayer
223.hook: a short surah after the Fatiha in the first two units
223.howItsDone: In each unit of the prayer Muslims recite al-Fatiha, and in the first two units they add a short surah or some verses, most often from Juz' 'Amma; the imam recites aloud at dawn, sunset and night, and silently at noon and afternoon.

segments.voice: Yesterday we turned around and saw Juz' 'Amma whole: the Day, the orphan, the soul, the One. Your line was the whole juz'. Which three surahs made your list? Day two hundred twenty-three.

Stand at the back of a mosque at sunset and listen. The imam's voice rises: first the Fatiha, the seven lines you've heard every time. Then a pause, and something else. Tonight it's a surah about daybreak. Tomorrow it might be the one about the elephant, or the orphan, or the soul. Around the room, people who couldn't order lunch in Arabic follow every word, because they learned these same short surahs as children. That's where Juz' 'Amma lives most of the time. Not on a shelf. In the mouths of people praying, five times a day, all over the world. Today: reciting in prayer, and why this little part gets said more than any other.
screen: `SUNSET, AT THE BACK OF A MOSQUE.` → `THE FATIHA, THEN SOMETHING ELSE.` → `WHERE JUZ' 'AMMA LIVES.`

segments.voice: Each prayer is made of units, rak'ahs: standing, bowing, prostrating, sitting. The dawn prayer has two, sunset three, the others four. In every unit, standing, the one praying recites the Fatiha. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in a hadith Bukhari records, that there is no prayer for the one who doesn't recite the opening of the Book. Then, in the first two units, something is added: a short surah, or a few verses from anywhere in the Qur'an. In the third and fourth units, the Fatiha alone. The schools of law weigh the addition differently: the Hanafi school counts it as required, and the others count it as a strongly recommended practice of the Prophet. At dawn, sunset and night, the imam recites aloud in the first two units; at noon and afternoon, silently. So people need a store of short surahs, and Juz' 'Amma is the store. Two stories show the spirit of it. One: a companion named Mu'adh led his people in prayer with such a long surah that a tired man left. The Prophet corrected him and named shorter ones instead, like By the sun and By the night. Two: another man, leading prayer, always added Say, He is Allah, the One, every single time. People complained. Asked why, he said it describes the Most Merciful, and he loved to recite it. The Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him. A short surah, said with love, is not a lesser prayer.
screen: `THE FATIHA IN EVERY UNIT.` · `A SHORT SURAH IN THE FIRST TWO.` · `MU'ADH IS TOLD: KEEP IT SHORTER.` · `THE MAN WHO LOVED AL-IKHLAS.` · then, large: `A NEW ONE TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose one short surah you don't yet know by heart. Al-Kawthar is the shortest, only three lines. Al-'Asr is three more. Read it slowly in whatever language you have, then read it again. On each breath, take one line and let it settle. If you pray, you can say it after the Fatiha in one of tonight's prayers, even if it comes out slowly and you need to glance at it. If you don't, you can simply listen to it recited once today. 224.title: Ayat al-Kursi
224.hook: the verse of the Throne: Allah, the Living, the Sustainer, neither drowsiness nor sleep (2:255)
224.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleep, after each obligatory prayer, and when leaving home for protection; it is one of the most widely memorized verses of the Qur'an and often hangs in calligraphy in homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: reciting in prayer, the Fatiha in every unit and a short surah in the first two. Your line was a new one tonight. Did a new surah get its first time last night? Day two hundred twenty-four.

Abu Hurayrah, a companion of the Prophet, was once put in charge of guarding the charity food. Bukhari tells the story. One night a man crept in and started taking handfuls. Abu Hurayrah grabbed him, heard a sad story about hungry children, and let him go. The next night, the same man. The same story. On the third night Abu Hurayrah wouldn't let go, and the thief offered a trade: let me go and I'll teach you words that will protect you. When you lie down to sleep, recite the verse of the Throne. Abu Hurayrah told the Prophet, who answered: he told you the truth, though he's a liar. Today we step out of Juz' 'Amma for a verse Muslims carry to bed. Ayat al-Kursi.
screen: `A GUARD, A THIEF, THREE NIGHTS.` → `A TRADE: WORDS FOR SLEEP.` → `HE TOLD YOU THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: It's verse two hundred fifty-five of Surah al-Baqarah, the second surah and the longest. Pickthall translates the opening like this: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Two names first. Al-Hayy, the Living, alive in a way that doesn't depend on anything. Al-Qayyum, which Pickthall calls the Eternal, means the one who stands by Himself and holds everything else up. Then the line our week has been circling. Four days ago An-Naba' told us sleep is a sign: we are made to stop, cut off, and come back. This verse says the one who holds everything up never does. Not even the first heaviness of the eyelids, sinah, the drowsiness before sleep, touches Him. Then the verse widens: to Him belongs everything in the heavens and the earth. No one intercedes with Him except by His permission. He knows what is before people and what is behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. Then the word that names the verse: kursi. In everyday Arabic a kursi is a chair. Pickthall says throne; many commentators say footstool, and one early explanation said it stands for His knowledge. The verse says it extends over the heavens and the earth, and guarding them doesn't tire Him. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asked a companion which verse in the Book of Allah is greatest. The answer he approved: this one. Our week in one picture: we held the self back, heard the great news, slept and woke, remembered the sorting, and all that time, someone stayed awake.
screen: `AL-HAYY, AL-QAYYUM.` · `NEITHER DROWSINESS NOR SLEEP.` · `KURSI — CHAIR, FOOTSTOOL, THRONE.` · `THE GREATEST VERSE.` · then, large: `HE DOES NOT SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Think of everything you're carrying that you'll have to put down tonight when you sleep: the unanswered emails, the person you're worried about, the thing that isn't fixed. Picture setting each one down, one per breath. You're allowed to stop. The verse says the one who holds it all doesn't. If you pray, you can recite Ayat al-Kursi tonight as you lie down, as Muslims have done since Abu Hurayrah's night watch. The bell holds the time.
Ayat al-Kursi. The verse of the Throne, al-Baqarah two fifty-five: the Living, the Sustainer, whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes. Today's word.
Your line: he does not sleep. Tonight, before sleep, read the verse, or just its first two lines, and let yourself put the day down. Day two hundred twenty-four.
